newsitem.title: USA: Chrysler Durango volume may hit 200,000/year.
newsitem.headline: Chrysler Durango volume may hit 200,000/year.

text.p: Chrysler Corp said Tuesday that production of its new 1998 Dodge Durango sport/utility vehicle could reach 200,000 units per year if consumer demand warrants.

In introducing the mid-size sport/utility vehicle at the North American International Auto Show here, Chrysler executives said the Durango's first year production volume is currently planned at about 120,000 to 160,000 units.
"We know how to get that up to 200,000 units if we need to," Chrysler Vice Chairman Robert Lutz told reporters.

Chrysler invested about $910 million in the Durango program: about $510 million in engineering for the vehicle and $400 million in the company's Newark, Del., plant, which will produce the vehicle. Much of the Newark investment went to install a new paint shop for the Durango.

The investment comes on top of a $500 million investment Chrysler made over the past two years to launch its new Dodge Dakota pick-up truck. The Durango uses the Dakota chassis, front end, instrument panel and engines.

Chrysler Chairman Robert Eaton said Chrysler developed the vehicle in 24 months, but the shortened lead time was due largely to the fact that it was based on the new generation Dakota platform. Chrysler still takes about 30 months to develop an all-new vehicle, he added.

The Durango will offer an optional third seat, allowing it to carry up to eight passengers. Chrysler claims the vehicle offers "more of everything," including larger engines, more room and towing capacity than current compact sport/utility vehicles including Ford Motor Co's Explorer and Chrysler's own Jeep Grand Cherokee.
Pricing was not announced, but analysts expect the Durango to be competitive with the Explorer and others.

Lutz said he believes Chrysler can maintain sales of Grand Cherokees at their current levels because the Durango is aimed at a different audience -- people with slightly lower incomes and "less buttoned up" than Grand Cherokee buyers.
He said the name was deliberately chosen to be "Marlboro-mannish," a reference to the rugged cigarette advertising pitchman.
Lutz said Chrysler will keep its Jeep dealers "fully competitive" on the product front.
